newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. submits welfare plan, key decisions lie ahead.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. submits welfare plan, key decisions lie ahead.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki on Wednesday submitted a brief outline of the state's welfare program to Washington that offered few hints about what sort of changes his Administration might seek later on.

Pataki did signal he plans to soften at least a few of the new federal rules. While the state has the option of limiting benefits for people to move to New York for one year, the state's plan sets a six-month limit, said Rus Sykes, deputy director of the State Community Aid Association in Albany.

And the Pataki Administration followed through on its promise to ensure qualified legal immigrants, who arrived before the federal bill became law on August 22, can keep Medicaid benefits, temporary aid and some other benefits.

There had been speculation the governor was considering whether or not to decentralize parts of the welfare system, perhaps by giving counties a greater say in handling the new workfare requirements imposed by the federal bill.

This issue was not clarified, as Pataki's statement said only that the bipartisan welfare task force, which analyzed all the state's options but did not make recommendations, addressed ways of giving localities more flexibility.

The governor, who this spring failed to get the Assembly to approve his welfare reforms, has said he plans to draft a bill that will set out how the state plans to modify its costly and complex program in the next several weeks.

He has said he plans to call a special legislative session around December to draft the new laws that will be required. That is when the key policy negotiations will occur, said state sources, who declined to be named.

New York followed the lead of a number of other states, who also submitted broad, preliminary plans. The states have until July 1 to finalize their programs, though Washington began accepting them on October 1. By sending the plans in early, states can ensure they get the biggest block grant possible, which for New York, totals almost $2.4 billion.

State souces said there were concerns that by sending in a broad plan, a step New York took only after being blasted for putting millions of dollars at risk by delaying, New York started the clock on new five-year time limits for benefits.

And sending in the broad plan also obliges New York to have all recipients in state-defined work programs after two years. Starting the clock before it finalized its program means the state might be at risk of incurring penalities if it fails to meet some of the new federal rules in the future, said the sources.
